title: DTCN-RevIN: A Densely Temporal Causal Network with reversible instance normalization for enhanced weather forecasting via multi-scale feature integration
content:
by Xixiang Yin, Sheng Shu, Minglei Yuan

Accurate weather forecasting is of paramount importance for disaster prevention, agriculture, and resource management, yet traditional Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) systems such as the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model face inherent limitations in temporal resolution and computational efficiency when capturing rapidly evolving atmospheric dynamics. Meanwhile, existing deep learning approaches—including Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCN), and Transformers—struggle with long-range temporal dependencies, distribution shift, and scalability. To address these challenges, this study proposes the Densely Temporal Causal Network with Reversible Instance Normalization (DTCN), a deep learning architecture that combines: (1) causal dilated convolutions for efficient temporal modeling, (2) dense inter-layer connections for enhanced feature propagation, (3) multi-scale feature integration, and critically, (4) RevIN standardization to address distribution shift in meteorological time series. Through 250 independent station-level model training runs (5 architectures × 10 stations × 5 random seeds), we systematically evaluate DTCN against four deep learning baseline architectures (TCN, LSTM, Transformer, and LSTM-Attention) for the 32→6 short-range forecasting configuration. Results show that: (i) DTCN achieves competitive top-tier overall performance, with RMSE of 0.0052 ± 0.0004 and R2 of 0.37 ± 0.06; (ii) DTCN matches TCN in rounded overall RMSE and R2, while showing slightly lower variance than TCN; (iii) all evaluated architectures achieve positive overall R2 with RevIN standardization (0.22–0.37); and (iv) per-variable results indicate variable-dependent advantages, with LSTM/LSTM-Attention performing best for temperature, TCN performing best for humidity, and DTCN remaining competitive across all three meteorological variables. These findings establish DTCN as a competitive data-driven alternative for short-range weather forecasting rather than an unambiguous winner across every metric and variable.
